title: Tailoring factors: what drives the choices
blurb: Name the seven tailoring factors and the outside influences that shape how PRINCE2 is applied.
question: A supplier will deliver a project using its own iterative-incremental framework, and the team is new to project work. Which tailoring factors are these, and how might they shape the way PRINCE2 is applied?

teach.body: Formally, PRINCE2 is tailored to suit the project's environment, size, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and level of risk. In plain English, before deciding how much control a project needs, look at seven things about it: where it sits, how big it is, how tangled it is, how much it matters, how the work will be done, how experienced the people are and how much could go wrong.

teach.caption: Every project has a CREST ID: seven facts about it that drive the tailoring choices.

head: Factor
The question
Typical tailoring effect
rows: Plan formality and level of detail
teach.caption: The effects are typical examples, not fixed rules. Several factors usually act together.

teach.body: Beyond the seven factors, several influences can cause a project to tailor the method. A commercial customer-supplier relationship may mean aligning processes, practices and documents with two or more quality systems. A programme may shape how the project is run. A supplier may want to use its own agile or iterative framework. And the organization may have its own standard project method that the project must start from.

teach.caption: Both feed 'agree the tailoring requirements', which tailors PRINCE2 for internal and external factors.

teach.body: Northmoor Water is replacing 40,000 household meters. Project manager Daniel Okafor reviews the factors. The project is large and important to the regulator relationship, so the board wants formal monthly reviews. The software supplier works iteratively, so quality activities are set to suit that approach. Two team managers are new to the role, so checkpoints are weekly. The company also has a standard project method, so Daniel tailors that and documents the deviations.

teach.caption: An illustration only: real tailoring weighs all seven factors, not just two.

teach.text: Delivery method is a tailoring factor, not a reason to drop PRINCE2. PRINCE2 is not specific to any industry, lifecycle or delivery method, so a supplier using an iterative or agile approach means the project tailors the method to fit it.

items: Seven factors: environment, size, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and level of risk (CREST ID).
Influences: commercial customer-supplier relationships, programme context, a supplier's own iterative framework and organizational standards.
A commercial relationship may require alignment with two or more quality systems.
A business's standard project method can itself be tailored; deviations are documented and agreed.
Factors shape how the method is applied, never whether the principles apply.

summary: You can now list the seven tailoring factors (environment, size, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and level of risk) and recognize which one a situation reflects. You can also name the influences from a project's setting, such as commercial relationships and organizational standards, that lead to tailoring.

A.q: Which of the following is a factor that PRINCE2 is tailored to suit?
options: The project's delivery method
The PM's personal preferences
The template used last time
The business layer's budget size
A.why: Delivery method is one of the seven tailoring factors, with environment, size, complexity, importance, team capability and level of risk (2.7).

whyNot.1: Tailoring is driven by features of the project, not by the project manager's personal style.
whyNot.2: Reusing an old template ignores the features of this project, which is what tailoring responds to.
whyNot.3: The size of the business layer's overall budget is not one of the seven tailoring factors.

A.q:
Which two are factors that PRINCE2 is tailored to suit?
1. Complexity
2. Importance
3. The sponsor's seniority
4. The number of practices
options: 2 and 3
1 and 2
3 and 4
1 and 4
A.why: Complexity and importance are both among the seven tailoring factors (2.7).

whyNot.0: Statement 3 is false: PRINCE2 has no sponsor role, and seniority is not a tailoring factor.
whyNot.2: Neither is a factor: there are always seven practices, and sponsor seniority is not listed.
whyNot.3: Statement 4 is false: the number of practices is fixed at seven, so it does not vary to suit the project.

A.q: A supplier will deliver the project using its own iterative-incremental framework. Which tailoring factor does this mainly reflect?
options: Importance
Scale of the project
Level of risk
Delivery method
A.why: How the products will be developed, here iteratively, is the delivery method factor (2.7, 1.5.3).

whyNot.0: Importance is about how much the project matters to the organization, not how the work is done.
whyNot.1: Size is the scale of the project, which the stem does not describe.
whyNot.2: Level of risk concerns how much could go wrong; the stem describes the way of working.

B.q: A project has a commercial customer-supplier relationship. What might this require when tailoring PRINCE2?
options: Asking the supplier to set the project tolerances
Using the supplier's business case as the project's
Aligning processes with both quality systems
Removing project assurance as the contract covers it
B.why: Where there is a commercial customer-supplier relationship, the project may need to align its processes, practices and documents with two or more quality systems (2.7).

whyNot.0: Project tolerances are set by the business layer, not by a supplier.
whyNot.1: The supplier has its own business case for taking part, but the project's business case is the customer's, owned by the executive.
whyNot.3: Project assurance remains a board responsibility; a contract does not remove it.

B.q: The team on a project has little experience of project work. How is this most likely to influence tailoring?
options: Fewer stages so the team is not overloaded
More frequent reporting and closer control
Removing checkpoint reports to save them time
Letting the team set its own stage tolerances
B.why: Team capability is a tailoring factor; an inexperienced team is a typical reason for more frequent reporting and closer control.

whyNot.0: Fewer stages reduce the board's decision points, which suits a simple, low-risk project rather than an inexperienced team.
whyNot.2: Removing checkpoints would reduce visibility just when the team needs closer support.
whyNot.3: Stage tolerances are set by the project board; an inexperienced team points to closer control, not more delegated authority.

B.q: Identify the missing word in the following sentence. Being part of a [?] is one of the influences that can lead a project to tailor PRINCE2.
options: work package
programme
quality review
checkpoint
B.why: Programme context is one of the influences that can cause a project to tailor the method (2.7, fig 1.2).

whyNot.0: A work package sits inside the project; it is not part of the project's wider context.
whyNot.2: A quality review is a quality control activity within the project, not a context.
whyNot.3: A checkpoint is a time-driven progress control within a work package, not a context.

C.q: Which statement about tailoring factors is correct?
options: Industry sector decides whether PRINCE2 can be used
Size changes the controls, while risk leaves them as they are
Importance changes the principles; complexity, the roles
Delivery method and team capability shape how it is applied
C.why: Delivery method and team capability are both tailoring factors that shape how PRINCE2 is applied (2.7).

whyNot.0: PRINCE2 is universal and not specific to any industry; sector influences tailoring, not suitability.
whyNot.1: Level of risk is one of the seven factors, so it also shapes the controls.
whyNot.2: No factor changes the principles; they apply to every PRINCE2 project.

C.q: A mid-sized internal project has many interdependent products and a newly formed, inexperienced team. Which two factors most justify more detailed plans and more frequent reports?
options: Complexity and team capability
Importance and size
Delivery method and environment
Size and delivery method
C.why: Many interdependent products describe complexity (more detailed plans), and an inexperienced team describes team capability (more frequent reporting) (2.7).

whyNot.1: The project is mid-sized and nothing is said about its importance, so neither factor explains the change.
whyNot.2: The stem says nothing about how the products are developed or about the organizational setting.
whyNot.3: Neither size nor delivery method is what the stem describes.

C.q: A local authority requires every project to use its own standard project method, which is based on PRINCE2. What should the project manager do in 'agree the tailoring requirements'?
options: Tailor the standard method and document agreed deviations
Replace the standard method with the full PRINCE2 manual
Apply the standard method and record no tailoring choices
Ask the team managers to pick which parts they will use
C.why: The project manager may need to tailor the business's standard project management approach for internal and external factors; any deviations must be documented and agreed (15.4.1).

whyNot.1: Organizational standards are a legitimate influence; the starting point is the business's own method.
whyNot.2: How the method is applied or tailored must be documented and agreed, even when it is the business's standard.
whyNot.3: The project manager leads this activity, and the board approves the result in the PID; team managers do not choose.

reteach.title: Read the project before you cut the cloth
reteach.question: If you were handed a project tomorrow, what seven things would you look at before deciding how much control it needs?

blocks.body: Where does it sit (environment)? How big is it (size)? How interlinked is the work (complexity)? How much does it matter (importance)? How will the products be made (delivery method)? How experienced are the people (team capability)? How much could go wrong (level of risk)? The answers tell you how to tailor.

steps.label: Ask the effect
steps.sub: what control does it call for?

blocks.text: Influences such as a commercial contract, a programme or a supplier's agile framework add to the seven factors. None of them lets a project drop a principle.

explain.body: Environment, size, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and level of risk. CREST ID is a quick way to recall them.

test.q: Which is NOT one of the seven tailoring factors?
options: The project's environment
The project's importance
The PM's preferred style
The level of risk
test.why: The seven factors are environment, size, complexity, importance, delivery method, team capability and level of risk; personal style is not one (2.7).

whyNot.0: Environment is one of the seven tailoring factors.
whyNot.1: Importance is one of the seven tailoring factors.
whyNot.3: Level of risk is one of the seven tailoring factors.

explain.h: Factors set the level of control
explain.body: A small, simple, low-risk project needs lighter controls; a large, complex or risky one needs more. A simple project with well-understood products may need only initiation plus one delivery stage.

explain.h: Factors push control up or down

test.q: A project is small, simple and low risk, with well-understood products. Which stage structure fits these factors?
options: Several delivery stages to spread the risk
Initiation plus a single delivery stage
Delivery stages with no initiation stage
One stage per product, each with a board
test.why: A simple project with few, well-understood products may need only two stages: initiation plus one delivery stage (7.2.3.1).

whyNot.0: Several delivery stages add decision points that a small, low-risk project does not need.
whyNot.2: Every PRINCE2 project has an initiation stage; the minimum is initiation plus one delivery stage.
whyNot.3: A project has one project board; stages are management decision points, not one per product.

explain.body: Commercial customer-supplier relationships, programme context, a supplier's own iterative framework and organizational standards can all cause tailoring.

test.q: Which is an influence that can cause a project to tailor PRINCE2?
options: A board member's wish to drop a principle
The team's wish to work without set roles
The PM's dislike of written reporting
A commercial customer-supplier relationship
test.why: A commercial customer-supplier relationship is a recognized influence; it may require alignment with two or more quality systems (2.7).

whyNot.0: Principles cannot be tailored away, so this is not a valid influence.
whyNot.1: PRINCE2 needs defined roles and responsibilities; working without them breaks a principle.
whyNot.2: Personal dislike is not an influence; reporting is tailored to the project's factors.

explain.body: Many businesses have their own standard project method. The project manager may tailor that standard for internal and external factors, and any deviation must be documented and agreed.

test.q: A business has its own standard project method. How is it treated when tailoring?
options: It is replaced by PRINCE2 before initiation
It overrides the principles where they conflict
It is tailored, with deviations documented and agreed
It is used as it stands, so no tailoring is needed
test.why: The project manager may tailor the business's standard project management approach; any deviations must be documented and agreed (15.4.1).

whyNot.0: The business's own method is the starting point; PRINCE2 does not demand it be replaced.
whyNot.1: Nothing overrides the principles on a PRINCE2 project.
whyNot.3: Even a standard method is adapted to the project, and that must be documented and agreed.
